examples.prompt: A gravity sewer normally conveys sewage without a pump in every pipe segment.
examples.explanation: Gravity flow uses elevation differences; lift stations serve low points.

examples.prompt: A force main is normally a pressurized discharge pipe from a pump station.
examples.explanation: Pumps add energy to convey wastewater through a force main.

examples.prompt: A failed check valve stuck open can let sewage return to a wet well after pumping stops.
examples.explanation: Reverse flow through a stuck-open check valve can recycle wastewater.

examples.prompt: A sudden increase in pump run time proves the pump is blocked.
examples.explanation: Inflow, population changes, and valve or pump restrictions can also change run time; investigate.

examples.prompt: A meter reading is more useful for diagnosis when compared with an established baseline.
examples.explanation: Trends and records help operators detect changes and potential malfunctions.

examples.prompt: Hydrogen sulfide can accumulate in low or enclosed sewer spaces.
examples.explanation: It is heavier than air and can collect in manholes and sewers.

examples.prompt: Wet-weather flow data can help identify possible infiltration and inflow problems.
examples.explanation: Comparing wet- and dry-weather flow helps prioritize investigation; it does not identify the exact entry point by itself.

examples.prompt: The purpose of a check valve is to reduce reverse flow.
examples.explanation: Check valves guard against backflow; debris may prevent closure.

examples.prompt: A lift-station high-level alarm should be treated as an indication for investigation.
examples.explanation: High level can signal pump or control problems and potential overflow risk.

examples.prompt: A single CCTV image alone establishes whether a sewer has enough wet-weather capacity.
examples.explanation: Capacity assessment also needs appropriate flow and system information.

examples.prompt: An asset inventory and current maps help plan collection-system maintenance.
examples.explanation: Knowing asset locations and condition supports prioritization and dispatch.

examples.prompt: A crew cleans 1,800 ft in 3 hours. The average cleaning rate is 600 ft/hour.
examples.explanation: Divide 1,800 ft by 3 hours to obtain 600 ft/hour.

examples.prompt: A wet well has 600 gallons of usable storage and a constant net filling rate of 20 gallons per minute. Time to fill is 30 minutes.
examples.explanation: 600 gallons divided by 20 gallons/minute equals 30 minutes, assuming constant net inflow.

examples.prompt: A lead-lag duplex station can alternate which pump starts first.
examples.explanation: Alternation shares the lead role across operating cycles.

examples.prompt: Match each term to its distinct description: Wet well, Force main, Check valve.
examples.explanation: Wet well: Collects wastewater before pumping; Force main: Conveys pumped wastewater under pressure; Check valve: Restricts reverse flow.

examples.prompt: In a duplex station with separate rising lead-start and higher lag-start setpoints, match each term to its distinct description.

pairs.right: Starts at the lead level in the described duplex system
Starts at the higher lag level when needed

examples.explanation: Lead pump: Starts at the lead level in the described duplex system; Lag pump: Starts at the higher lag level when needed; High-level alarm: Signals unusually high wet-well level.

examples.prompt: Match each term to its distinct description: Preventive maintenance, Predictive maintenance, Emergency maintenance.

pairs.right: Scheduled servicing based on time or usage
Uses condition data to anticipate failure and schedule work
Immediate work responding to an urgent failure

examples.explanation: Preventive maintenance: Scheduled servicing based on time or usage; Predictive maintenance: Uses condition data to anticipate failure and schedule work; Emergency maintenance: Immediate work responding to an urgent failure.

examples.prompt: Match each term to its distinct description: CCTV inspection, Smoke testing, Flow monitoring.
examples.explanation: CCTV inspection: Visual record inside a sewer; Smoke testing: Tracing smoke escaping from openings; Flow monitoring: Measuring wastewater flow over time.

examples.prompt: Match each term to its distinct description: Operating budget, Capital plan, Work order.

pairs.right: Record of a specific job and its status

examples.explanation: Operating budget: Recurring operating expenses; Capital plan: Major long-term infrastructure investments; Work order: Record of a specific job and its status.

examples.prompt: Match each term to its distinct description: Float switch, Hour meter, Pressure gauge.
examples.explanation: Float switch: Level-triggered switch; Hour meter: Records accumulated motor running time; Pressure gauge: Indicates pressure in a line.

examples.prompt: Match each term to its distinct description: Manhole, Gravity sewer, Pump station.

pairs.right: Facility lifting wastewater to a higher elevation

examples.explanation: Manhole: Access structure to underground sewer; Gravity sewer: Pipe conveying wastewater using grade; Pump station: Facility lifting wastewater to a higher elevation.

examples.prompt: Match each term to its distinct description: Infiltration, Inflow, Exfiltration.

pairs.right: Surface water entering through direct openings
Wastewater leaking out of the sewer

examples.explanation: Infiltration: Groundwater entering through defects; Inflow: Surface water entering through direct openings; Exfiltration: Wastewater leaking out of the sewer.

examples.prompt: Match each term to its distinct description: Generator, Transfer switch, Portable bypass pump.
examples.explanation: Generator: Supplies standby electrical power; Transfer switch: Changes the station power source; Portable bypass pump: Moves wastewater around unavailable equipment.

examples.prompt: Match each atmospheric measurement to the quantity reported; these measurements can be made by a multigas meter.

pairs.right: Reports combustible atmosphere as a percentage of the lower flammable limit
Reports H₂S concentration in parts per million

examples.explanation: Oxygen-content measurement: Reports oxygen concentration by volume; Combustible-gas measurement: Reports combustible atmosphere as a percentage of the lower flammable limit; Hydrogen sulfide measurement: Reports H₂S concentration in parts per million.

examples.prompt: Match each specified rehabilitation approach to its distinct description.

pairs.right: Installs a continuous liner throughout a manhole-to-manhole pipe reach
Repairs a short, identified defective section only
Breaks existing pipe while pulling in a replacement along its route

examples.explanation: Full-reach pipe lining: Installs a continuous liner throughout a manhole-to-manhole pipe reach; Localized spot repair: Repairs a short, identified defective section only; Pipe bursting: Breaks existing pipe while pulling in a replacement along its route.

examples.prompt: Match each term to its distinct description: Asset map, Maintenance log, Alarm record.
examples.explanation: Asset map: Shows infrastructure locations; Maintenance log: Records work and equipment history; Alarm record: Records abnormal operating alerts.

examples.prompt: Match each term to its distinct description: Wet-weather comparison, Pump drawdown test, Motor hour meter.

pairs.right: Highlights a possible rain-related flow response

examples.explanation: Wet-weather comparison: Highlights a possible rain-related flow response; Pump drawdown test: Estimates pump delivery rate; Motor hour meter: Records cumulative run time.

examples.prompt: Which item is not a way to inspect or trace a sewer?
examples.explanation: An hour meter records pump run time; the others help inspect or trace sewer pathways.

examples.prompt: Which is not a wet-well level-sensing device?
examples.explanation: A check valve limits reverse flow; the other devices sense wet-well level.

examples.prompt: Which is not a potential cause of a sanitary sewer overflow?
examples.explanation: Blockage, power loss, and insufficient capacity can contribute to overflows.

examples.prompt: Which item is not an atmospheric hazard in a sewer?
examples.explanation: An external ladder is not an atmospheric hazard; the other choices are.

examples.prompt: Which is not a physical collection-system asset?
examples.explanation: The spreadsheet can record assets but is not a physical collection-system asset.

examples.prompt: Which is not a potential source of unwanted water entering a sanitary sewer?
examples.explanation: The other defects can admit groundwater or runoff; a sealed discharge valve is not an entry path.

examples.prompt: Which item does not supply emergency power?
examples.explanation: A check valve controls reverse flow; the others are possible power sources.

examples.prompt: A station has 400 gallons of available storage up to its first spill point. The constant net filling rate is 20 gallons/minute and there is no other storage or outlet. Which proposed time to spill is incorrect?
examples.explanation: 400 ÷ 20 = 20 minutes, equal to 1,200 seconds and one-third hour.

examples.prompt: Which action is not a planned maintenance practice?

options.label: Waiting for an overflow before responding

examples.explanation: Planned work aims to detect or prevent failure rather than only reacting.

examples.prompt: Which item is not an element of a simple risk ranking?
examples.explanation: Failure likelihood and consequence, supported by condition evidence, help rank assets.

examples.prompt: Which is not a hydraulic component of a conventional wet-well station?
examples.explanation: A timesheet documents labor; the other choices are wastewater conveyance components.

examples.prompt: Which item does not help verify an abnormal high-level alarm?

options.label: Compare level with an independent reading
Inspect the alarm and sensor under site procedures

examples.explanation: Verification combines observed level, controls, and pump status; deletion is not a diagnostic check.

examples.prompt: Which item is not a document for locating sewer assets?
examples.explanation: A nameplate identifies motor characteristics; maps and drawings describe locations.

examples.prompt: Which is not a physical sewer rehabilitation method?
examples.explanation: The first three are repair or renewal methods; time sheet approval is administrative.

examples.prompt: Which is not normally a warning sign used for pump troubleshooting?

options.label: The color of the operator’s lunchbox

examples.explanation: Operational measurements and alarms can indicate change; lunchbox color has no such relationship.

examples.prompt: Which is not a normal objective of a collection-system maintenance program?
examples.explanation: Inspections help reveal deterioration and support maintenance planning.

examples.prompt: Heavy rain enters a sanitary system through a damaged cover. What operating effect is plausible?

options.label: Lower pump demand in every case

examples.explanation: Runoff entering the system adds hydraulic load and may increase pumping.

examples.prompt: During a power outage all station pumps stop, positive inflow continues, and there is no other outlet. Before any overflow, what happens to wet-well level?
examples.explanation: With no outflow, continuing positive inflow increases stored volume and level before overflow.

examples.prompt: A pump is partially blocked by debris. What trend can result?
examples.explanation: Reduced pump delivery can increase time needed to lower the wet well.

examples.prompt: A pump removes a net 300 gallons from a wet well in 3 minutes while inflow is zero. What is its average discharge?
examples.explanation: With zero inflow, discharge equals 300 gallons divided by 3 minutes.

examples.prompt: During a 5-minute drawdown, wet-well storage falls by 400 gallons while inflow is a constant 20 gallons/minute. What is average pump discharge?
examples.explanation: Net drawdown is 400 ÷ 5 = 80 gallons/minute. Add the 20 gallons/minute inflow to obtain 100.

examples.prompt: Before any overflow, a station receives 80 gallons/minute and a bypass removes 50 gallons/minute; there are no other inflows or outflows. How fast does stored volume increase?
examples.explanation: Net filling is inflow minus bypass flow: 80 − 50 = 30 gallons/minute.

examples.prompt: A working pump hour meter, with no reset or rollover, reads 1,220 hours today and 1,100 hours last week. How long did it run during the interval?
examples.explanation: Subtract the earlier cumulative meter reading from the later one: 1,220 − 1,100 = 120 hours.

examples.prompt: An operator compares pump run-hour logs over time. What can a marked unexplained increase prompt?

options.label: Investigate changing inflow or equipment condition
Assume the meter is a flow meter

examples.explanation: Higher run time has multiple possible causes, including I/I and restrictions.

examples.prompt: Groundwater enters through a cracked sewer joint. What does that add to the system?
examples.explanation: Infiltration is water entering through defects from surrounding ground.

examples.prompt: Wastewater leaks from a defective pipe into surrounding soil. What is the process?
examples.explanation: Exfiltration means wastewater leaves the pipe through a defect.

examples.prompt: A calibrated pressure gauge trends lower on a force main, all else comparable. What is one possible cause to investigate?
examples.explanation: A decrease can indicate a leak, but a reading alone does not prove one.

examples.prompt: An alternating duplex station changes the lead pump each cycle. What is the intended operational benefit?

options.label: Ensure both pumps are always on

examples.explanation: Alternation distributes lead operation rather than using one pump for every start.

examples.prompt: A bypass pump actually discharges less than the continuing upstream inflow. With no other outlet and before any spill, what can happen to upstream storage?
examples.explanation: If inflow exceeds bypass discharge, stored wastewater increases.

examples.prompt: A pump’s off level is set too close to its start level. What may occur?
examples.explanation: A narrow operating range may produce frequent starts and stops; settings must suit the station.

examples.prompt: A rising trend of repeat blockages occurs on one pipe segment. What management action is justified?

options.label: Remove the segment from the asset map
Assume all other segments are blocked

examples.explanation: Repeated failures justify examining the segment and adapting maintenance.

examples.prompt: A station is checked only after failure and spare parts are not available. What outcome becomes more likely?
examples.explanation: Prepared inventories and planned maintenance support timely restoration.

examples.prompt: A supervisor says: “The manhole smells normal, so no atmospheric testing is needed.” What is the flaw?

options.label: Relying on smell to rule out gas

examples.explanation: Smell cannot reliably detect hydrogen sulfide; follow the site entry program.

examples.prompt: A crew enters a sewer to rescue a coworker without training or protection. Find the flaw.
examples.explanation: Untrained rescue attempts can produce additional victims.

examples.prompt: A manager deletes recurring high-level alarms without reviewing them. Find the flaw.
examples.explanation: Repeated alarms can indicate control or pumping problems and merit investigation.

examples.prompt: An operator reports a pump drawdown rate as the pump delivery while ignoring substantial inflow during the test. Find the flaw.

options.label: Omitting inflow from the volume balance

examples.explanation: Pump discharge equals the observed volume decrease per time plus simultaneous inflow, if rates are steady.

examples.prompt: A crew uses an old map after a recorded pipe relocation without checking updates. Find the flaw.
examples.explanation: Updated maps and field verification reduce errors about asset location.

examples.prompt: A supervisor classifies every backup as a capacity problem without checking for blockage. Find the flaw.
examples.explanation: Both blockages and insufficient capacity may cause backups.

examples.prompt: A planner divides 600 gallons of available storage up to the first spill point by 40 gallons/minute inflow to estimate 15 minutes to spill. A bypass continuously removes 10 gallons/minute, and there are no other inflows or outlets. What is the flaw?
examples.explanation: The net filling rate is 40 − 10 = 30 gallons/minute, so the estimate is 20 minutes if rates stay constant.

examples.prompt: A utility chooses a rehabilitation method solely from pipe age, ignoring inspection and consequences. Find the flaw.
examples.explanation: Age is useful but condition and failure consequences also inform priorities.

examples.prompt: A crew assumes a drop in force-main pressure proves a leak without further checks. Find the flaw.

options.label: Treating an indicator as conclusive proof

examples.explanation: Pressure change is a clue, not a stand-alone diagnosis.

examples.prompt: An operator changes an alarm setpoint to hide repeated high levels without investigating. Find the flaw.

options.label: Masking the symptom instead of addressing its cause

examples.explanation: Investigate whether the alarm reflects a real condition or a sensor issue.

examples.prompt: A planner forecasts a one-hour outage will be safe without comparing available storage and net inflow. Find the flaw.
examples.explanation: Time to overflow depends on available volume and net rate of filling.

examples.prompt: A station has a known first spill elevation at its wet well. An operator counts volume above that elevation as available emergency storage. Find the flaw.
examples.explanation: In this example the first spill point limits storage; in an actual system check for lower upstream overflow points too.

examples.prompt: A supervisor records a spill estimate but omits the time and basis used. Find the flaw.
examples.explanation: Time, measurements, and assumptions allow the estimate to be reviewed and improved.

examples.prompt: A gravity sewer drops from an upstream invert elevation of 152.4 ft to a downstream invert elevation of 148.8 ft over a horizontal run of 600 ft. What is the downward grade as a percentage?
examples.explanation: Grade (%) = vertical drop ÷ horizontal run × 100. The drop is 152.4 ft − 148.8 ft = 3.6 ft. Divide 3.6 ft by 600 ft to get 0.006 ft/ft; multiply by 100 to obtain a 0.6% downward grade.

examples.prompt: A rectangular sewer flow channel is 1.5 ft wide, with water 1.0 ft deep and a measured cross-sectional average velocity of 2.2 ft/s. Estimate the flow rate.
examples.explanation: Use Q = A × v, where Q is flow in ft³/s, A is wetted cross-sectional area in ft², and v is average velocity in ft/s. A = width × water depth = 1.5 ft × 1.0 ft = 1.5 ft². Thus Q = 1.5 ft² × 2.2 ft/s = 3.3 ft³/s.

examples.prompt: A vertical cylindrical wet well has an internal diameter of 8 ft. From the current level to the first spill elevation, the level can rise 3 ft. Assume no other connected storage, use 0.7854 for π/4 and 7.48 gal/ft³, and neglect internal obstructions. Approximately how much storage is available?
examples.explanation: Cylindrical storage volume = (π/4) × diameter² × available rise. The cross-sectional area is 0.7854 × (8 ft)² = 50.2656 ft². Multiply by 3 ft to get 150.7968 ft³. Convert to gallons: 150.7968 ft³ × 7.48 gal/ft³ = 1,127.96 gal, or approximately 1,128 gal. The first spill point and connected storage must be verified at an actual site.

examples.prompt: A wastewater pump delivers 396 gal/min against 50 ft of total dynamic head. Assuming water-like density and pump efficiency of 62.5%, approximately what brake horsepower is required at the pump shaft? Use 3,960 as the US-unit conversion factor.
examples.explanation: First find water horsepower: WHP = flow (gal/min) × total head (ft) ÷ 3,960 = 396 × 50 ÷ 3,960 = 5 hp. Convert pump efficiency from 62.5% to 0.625. Brake horsepower = WHP ÷ pump efficiency = 5 hp ÷ 0.625 = 8 hp. This is pump-shaft power, not electrical input or a motor selection; motor losses and selection margin are separate.

examples.prompt: In a controlled tracer test, dye travels 540 ft between manholes. After injection, it first appears at the downstream manhole at 150 seconds and is last visible at 210 seconds. Using the midpoint of those times as an approximate travel time, what velocity does the midpoint method estimate?
examples.explanation: Midpoint travel time = (first-arrival time + last-visible time) ÷ 2 = (150 s + 210 s) ÷ 2 = 180 s. Estimated velocity = distance ÷ midpoint time = 540 ft ÷ 180 s = 3.0 ft/s. The midpoint method is an approximation; first and last detection alone do not establish a concentration-weighted mean travel time or uniform velocity.

examples.prompt: A three-person sewer-cleaning crew works 7 hours. Each person costs $32 per hour, and the cleaning truck costs $120 per hour for those same 7 hours. The crew cleans 2,100 ft. Excluding all other costs, what is the combined labor-and-truck cost per foot?
examples.explanation: Labor cost = 3 workers × 7 h × $32/(worker·h) = $672. Truck cost = 7 h × $120/h = $840. Total specified cost = $672 + $840 = $1,512. Unit cost = $1,512 ÷ 2,100 ft = $0.72/ft. Other overhead or materials are excluded by assumption.

examples.prompt: A lift-station motor draws a constant measured electrical input of 18 kW for 8 hours. If the energy charge is $0.14 per kWh, what is the energy charge for this run, ignoring demand charges and taxes?
examples.explanation: Energy = measured electrical power × operating time = 18 kW × 8 h = 144 kWh. Energy charge = 144 kWh × $0.14/kWh = $20.16. Because electrical input is already specified in kW, do not apply a horsepower conversion or an additional efficiency factor.

examples.prompt: For a simplified force-main calculation, a 300-ft length of 12-inch internal-diameter pipe is completely full. At a constant flow of 120 gal/min, what is its theoretical volume divided by flow, in minutes? Use π/4 = 0.7854 and 7.48 gal/ft³.
examples.explanation: Convert diameter: 12 in ÷ 12 in/ft = 1 ft. Pipe volume = (π/4) × diameter² × length = 0.7854 × (1 ft)² × 300 ft = 235.62 ft³. Convert: 235.62 ft³ × 7.48 gal/ft³ = 1,762.44 gal. Theoretical volume/flow time = 1,762.44 gal ÷ 120 gal/min = 14.69 min, approximately 14.7 min. Real travel times can differ because of flow variation and mixing.

examples.prompt: A cylindrical wet well has a 4-ft internal diameter. With the pump off, its level rises 0.50 ft in 2 min; with the pump running, its level still rises 0.75 ft in 5 min. Assume constant equal inflow during both periods, constant actual discharge, no other flows, and use π/4 = 0.7854 and 7.48 gal/ft³. Approximately what is the pump discharge?
examples.explanation: First find well area: A = 0.7854 × (4 ft)² = 12.5664 ft². Each foot of level change represents 12.5664 ft² × 1 ft × 7.48 gal/ft³ = 93.996672 gal. With the pump off, inflow = 93.996672 gal/ft × 0.50 ft ÷ 2 min = 23.499168 gal/min. With the pump on, net accumulation = 93.996672 gal/ft × 0.75 ft ÷ 5 min = 14.0995008 gal/min. Since accumulation = inflow − pump discharge, pump discharge = 23.499168 − 14.0995008 = 9.3996672 gal/min, approximately 9.4 gal/min.

examples.prompt: In a wet-well lift station served by a gravity sewer and discharging to a force main, does the wastewater reach the gravity sewer inlet before or after the force main?
examples.explanation: Wastewater from the gravity sewer enters the wet well, and the pump sends it into the force main. This is the stated wet-well arrangement, not every pumping design.

examples.prompt: In the Minnesota manual’s lot-level low-pressure sewer arrangement, does wastewater enter the holding tank before or after the gravity pipe from the building?
examples.explanation: The building drain connects by gravity sewer to the lot holding tank; the tank stores wastewater for the grinder pump. Other collection configurations can differ.

examples.prompt: In a lot-level low-pressure sewer with a holding tank and grinder pump, does wastewater pass the grinder pump before or after entering the pressurized main?
examples.explanation: The grinder pump grinds solids and pressurizes the wastewater that then enters the pressure main. This describes the low-pressure system in the Minnesota training manual.

examples.prompt: In an ordinary resin-impregnated cured-in-place pipe rehabilitation, is the liner cured before or after it is positioned inside the host pipe?
examples.explanation: The resin-impregnated liner is inserted and held against the host pipe, then cured into a solid liner. EPA discusses different insertion and curing techniques.

examples.prompt: In Portland’s CIPP process for a mainline sewer, is reopening service laterals covered by the liner before or after curing the liner?
examples.explanation: Portland describes curing the installed liner first and then reopening the lateral connections that the liner covered. Project specifications and conditions control the work.

examples.prompt: For a gravity sewer selected for CIPP using EPA’s described planning process, is the host-pipe condition examination before or after the relining work?
examples.explanation: EPA describes examining the host pipe, typically with CCTV, and collecting measurements ahead of relining to inform the choice and design of the liner.

examples.prompt: In Portland’s illustrated pipe-bursting method, does reconnection of existing laterals to the replacement main occur before or after placement of that replacement main?
examples.explanation: The replacement main must be pulled into place before existing lateral connections can be connected to it. Portland describes a specific method rather than a universal project sequence.

examples.prompt: For Portland’s pipe-bursting approach, is temporary disconnection of the existing service laterals from the old main before or after the bursting operation?
examples.explanation: Portland describes disconnecting laterals and providing temporary service connections ahead of bursting the existing main. A project’s engineered plan governs the actual approach.

examples.prompt: In Portland’s open-trench sewer replacement example, is installing the replacement main before or after removing the old pipe section?
examples.explanation: The city describes exposing and removing the existing pipe, installing the replacement and backfilling. The answer refers to this open-trench method.

examples.prompt: In Portland’s spot-repair example, is permanent pavement restoration before or after the repair passes inspection?
examples.explanation: Portland describes replacing the damaged section and applying a temporary patch; permanent repaving occurs after the repair passes inspection.

examples.prompt: In Portland’s example involving a collapsed sewer section and a mainline CIPP liner, is a spot repair of that section performed before or after the liner is installed?
examples.explanation: In this specific application, replacing a collapsed or severely deteriorated section prepares the mainline for the subsequent trenchless liner. Spot repair is not necessary on every lining project.

examples.prompt: In the Minnesota manual’s conventional sewer televising procedure, is normal line cleaning before or after the CCTV inspection?
examples.explanation: The manual says sewer lines are normally cleaned before televising so the camera can travel and show pipe condition. Screening methods and project conditions may differ.

examples.prompt: In EPA’s condition-assessment approach using both stationary zoom cameras and conventional CCTV on a selected pipe segment, is the zoom-camera inspection before or after the detailed conventional CCTV inspection?
examples.explanation: EPA describes stationary zoom-camera inspection as a rapid screening method to prioritize segments for subsequent detailed conventional CCTV or cleaning. It need not replace CCTV.

examples.prompt: In EPA’s example involving a large basin with poor infiltration and inflow performance, were strategically placed flow meters deployed before or after low-infiltration-and-inflow sub-basins were screened out of further condition assessment?
examples.explanation: In EPA’s example, the utility subdivided the basin and used strategically placed flow meters to identify areas with low infiltration and inflow, which it could then exclude from further condition assessment. The sequence describes that example, not every study.

examples.prompt: In the older mechanical wet-well float control described in Minnesota’s collection manual, is energizing the motor starter before or after the float-actuated switch closes?
examples.explanation: In the described mechanical controller, a rising float ultimately closes the switch, which energizes the motor starter and starts the pump. Actual control hardware and interlocks vary by station.
